chapters.title: The reader and his two transmitters
paragraphs: The reader: Khalaf ibn Hishām ibn Thaʿlab al-Asadī al-Bazzār al-Baghdādī, Abū Muḥammad (150–229 AH), a Kūfan reader known as Khalaf al-ʿĀshir, 'the tenth'. He is the same Khalaf who transmits the qirāʾah of Ḥamzah, but what is described here is his own independent reading, one of the three that complete the ten.

The transmitters: Isḥāq ibn Ibrāhīm ibn ʿUthmān al-Marwazī, Abū Yaʿqūb (d. 286 AH), and Idrīs ibn ʿAbd al-Karīm al-Ḥaddād al-Baghdādī, Abū al-Ḥasan (d. 292 AH). The source records no difference between them in the uṣūl, so every rule below holds for both Isḥāq and Idrīs.

The way: al-Durrah al-Muḍiyyah of Ibn al-Jazarī. The poem treats Ḥamzah as Khalaf's base reading and mentions only where Khalaf departs from it; where it is silent he reads as Ḥamzah does. For this reason many rules below are stated by comparison with Ḥamzah as well as with Ḥafṣ.

chapters.title: The basmalah between two sūrahs
paragraphs: Between two sūrahs: Khalaf joins the end of one sūrah directly to the beginning of the next without the basmalah (waṣl), applying whatever tajwīd rule the junction requires. This is the only way given for him; Ḥafṣ separates the two sūrahs with the basmalah.
From al-Nās to al-Fātiḥah: here the basmalah must be read.

chapters.title: Sūrat al-Fātiḥah
paragraphs: The basmalah: he counts it as the first āyah of al-Fātiḥah, as Ḥafṣ does.
مَالِكِ: with an alif after the mīm, مَالِكِ يَوْمِ الدِّينِ (1:4), like Ḥafṣ.
الصِّرَاطَ: with a pure ṣād, الصِّرَاطَ الْمُسْتَقِيمَ (1:6) and صِرَاطَ الَّذِينَ (1:7), like Ḥafṣ and unlike his base reading; this holds wherever the word occurs, definite or indefinite.
Hāʾ of عَلَيْهِمْ: with kasrah in عَلَيْهِمْ, إِلَيْهِمْ and لَدَيْهِمْ, like Ḥafṣ, where Ḥamzah gives the hāʾ a ḍammah.

chapters.title: Mīm al-jamʿ and the hāʾ before it
paragraphs: Before a vowelled letter: the mīm is read with sukūn and without ṣilah, as in أَلَّا خَوْفٌ عَلَيْهِمْ وَلَا هُمْ يَحْزَنُونَ (3:170), like Ḥafṣ.
Before a sākin, in general: like all readers he gives the mīm a passing ḍammah without ṣilah, as in مِنْهُمُ الْمُؤْمِنُونَ (3:110) and عَلَيْكُمُ الْقِتَالُ (2:216).

Before a sākin when the hāʾ follows a kasrah or a yāʾ sākinah: he reads both the hāʾ and the mīm with ḍammah, as Ḥamzah does: عَلَيْهُمُ الْقِتَالُ (2:246), بِهُمُ الْأَسْبَابُ (2:166), قِبْلَتِهُمُ الَّتِي (2:142). Ḥafṣ keeps the kasrah of the hāʾ: عَلَيْهِمُ الْقِتَالُ.
On stopping: the hāʾ returns to kasrah, عَلَيْهِمْ.

chapters.title: Hāʾ al-kināyah
paragraphs: General rule: Khalaf lengthens the pronoun hāʾ with ṣilah in the same way as Ḥafṣ; the words below are those in which the two differ.
فَأَلْقِهِۦ: kasrah with ṣilah in فَأَلْقِهِۦ إِلَيْهِمْ (27:28); Ḥafṣ reads فَأَلْقِهْ with sukūn.
وَيَتَّقِهِۦ: kasrah on the qāf and ṣilah of the hāʾ (24:52); Ḥafṣ alone reads وَيَتَّقْهِ with a sākin qāf and a short hāʾ.
أَرْجِهِۦ: kasrah with ṣilah in أَرْجِهِۦ وَأَخَاهُ (7:111 and 26:36); Ḥafṣ reads أَرْجِهْ.
يَرْضَهُۥ: ḍammah with ṣilah in يَرْضَهُۥ لَكُمْ (39:7); Ḥafṣ reads the ḍammah short.
لِأَهْلِهِ امْكُثُوا: kasrah of the hāʾ (20:10 and 28:29), like Ḥafṣ; Ḥamzah reads it with ḍammah.

أَنسَانِيهِ and عَلَيْهِ اللَّهَ: kasrah of the hāʾ in وَمَا أَنسَانِيهِ إِلَّا الشَّيْطَانُ (18:63) and بِمَا عَاهَدَ عَلَيْهِ اللَّهَ (48:10), the lām of the Divine Name in the second being thin. Ḥafṣ alone reads both with ḍammah, أَنسَانِيهُ and عَلَيْهُ اللَّهَ, with a heavy lām.
فِيهِ مُهَانًا: the hāʾ is short in وَيَخْلُدْ فِيهِ مُهَانًا (25:69); Ḥafṣ lengthens it with ṣilah.

chapters.title: Madd and qaṣr
paragraphs: Madd muttaṣil and madd munfaṣil: both are read with tawassuṭ, four ḥarakāt, as in جَاءَ and بِمَا أُنزِلَ (2:4). The source counts this among the rules in which Khalaf agrees with Ḥafṣ.
Madd badal and līn: the Durrah study adds that he reads madd badal with qaṣr, as in ءَامَنُوا and أُوتُوا, and does not lengthen a līn letter before hamzah, as in شَيْءٍ.

chapters.title: The hamzahs
paragraphs: Two hamzahs in one word: both are fully pronounced (taḥqīq), as in ءَأَنذَرْتَهُمْ (2:6). This includes ءَأَعْجَمِيٌّ وَعَرَبِيٌّ (41:44), where Ḥafṣ reads the second hamzah with tashīl.

Added interrogative hamzah: he reads a question, with two realised hamzahs, where Ḥafṣ reads a statement, in ءَأَٰمَنتُمْ (7:123, 20:71, 26:49), أَئِنَّ لَنَا لَأَجْرًا (7:113) and أَئِنَّكُمْ لَتَأْتُونَ الْفَاحِشَةَ (29:28); the next āyah, أَئِنَّكُمْ لَتَأْتُونَ الرِّجَالَ (29:29), is a question for both.
Two hamzahs in two words: both with taḥqīq, as in جَاءَ أَمْرُنَا, like Ḥafṣ.
Ibdāl: the sākin hamzah becomes an alif in يَاجُوجَ وَمَاجُوجَ (18:94, 21:96) and a yāʾ in الذِّيبُ (12:13, 14, 17). Ḥafṣ reads يَأْجُوجَ وَمَأْجُوجَ and الذِّئْبُ with hamzah.

Naql: he moves the fatḥah of the hamzah to the sīn and drops the hamzah only in the imperative of saʾala after wāw or fāʾ: وَسَلِ الْقَرْيَةَ (12:82), فَسَلُوا أَهْلَ الذِّكْرِ (16:43), وَسَلْهُمْ عَنِ الْقَرْيَةِ (7:163). Ḥafṣ reads وَاسْأَلِ and فَاسْأَلُوا.
Dropped hamzah: يُضَاهُونَ (9:30), with ḍammah on the hāʾ and no hamzah; Ḥafṣ reads يُضَاهِئُونَ.

Words read with a hamzah: جَبْرَئِيلَ (2:97; Ḥafṣ جِبْرِيلَ), مِيكَائِيلَ (2:98; Ḥafṣ مِيكَالَ), دَكَّاءَ in al-Aʿrāf (7:143; Ḥafṣ دَكًّا), and هُزْؤًا and كُفْؤًا (112:4) with a sākin middle letter and a hamzah, where Ḥafṣ reads هُزُوًا and كُفُوًا.
Hamzah on stopping: he keeps the hamzah with taḥqīq when stopping and does not lighten it as Ḥamzah does.

chapters.title: Sakt
paragraphs: The four sakt places of Ḥafṣ: Khalaf, like all readers other than Ḥafṣ, joins without sakt: عِوَجًا قَيِّمًا (18:1–2) with ikhfāʾ of the tanwīn, مَرْقَدِنَا هَٰذَا (36:52), and مَن رَّاقٍ (75:27) and بَل رَّانَ (83:14) with idghām; he also reads رَانَ with imālah.
Sakt before hamzah: he leaves the sakt that Ḥamzah makes on a sākin before hamzah, reading straight through in words such as مَنْ ءَامَنَ, وَبِالْآخِرَةِ and شَيْءٍ.
Isḥāq and Idrīs: by the way of the Durrah neither transmitter has sakt. The sakt reported from Idrīs belongs to the way of the Ṭayyibah and is not part of this way.

chapters.title: Idghām and iẓhār
paragraphs: Idghām kabīr: he does not merge two vowelled letters. He reads with iẓhār the places in which idghām is transmitted from Ḥamzah: وَالصَّافَّاتِ صَفًّا (37:1), فَالزَّاجِرَاتِ زَجْرًا (37:2), فَالتَّالِيَاتِ ذِكْرًا (37:3), وَالذَّارِيَاتِ ذَرْوًا (51:1), فَالْمُلْقِيَاتِ ذِكْرًا (77:5), فَالْمُغِيرَاتِ صُبْحًا (100:3), بَيَّتَ طَائِفَةٌ (4:81), and أَتُمِدُّونَنِ بِمَالٍ (27:36) with two separate nūns. In all of these he agrees with Ḥafṣ.
Dāl of qad: merged into eight letters, sīn, dhāl, ḍād, ẓāʾ, zāy, jīm, ṣād and shīn: قَد سَّمِعَ (58:1), فَقَد ظَّلَمَ (2:231), قَد جَّاءَكُمْ. Ḥafṣ reads all of these with iẓhār.
Dhāl of idh: merged into tāʾ and dāl only, out of its six letters: إِذ تَّمْشِي (20:40), إِذ تَّلَقَّوْنَهُ (24:15), إِذ دَّخَلُوا (15:52). Ḥafṣ reads iẓhār.

Tāʾ al-taʾnīth: merged into five letters, sīn, ṣād, zāy, ẓāʾ and jīm: وَجَاءَت سَّيَّارَةٌ (12:19), حَصِرَت صُّدُورُهُمْ (4:90), نَضِجَت جُّلُودُهُمْ (4:56). Before thāʾ he reads iẓhār, كَذَّبَتْ ثَمُودُ, departing from Ḥamzah. Ḥafṣ reads iẓhār before all six.
Lām of hal and bal: iẓhār before all of its letters, as in بَلْ تُؤْثِرُونَ (87:16) and هَلْ تَرَىٰ (67:3), like Ḥafṣ.

Bāʾ into mīm: he merges the sākin bāʾ in وَيُعَذِّب مَّن يَشَاءُ (2:284), where he reads the verb in the jussive; Ḥafṣ reads وَيُعَذِّبُ with ḍammah. In ارْكَبْ مَعَنَا (11:42) he reads iẓhār, whereas Ḥafṣ merges.

Dhāl into tāʾ: merged in عُذتُّ (40:27, 44:20), فَنَبَذتُّهَا (20:96), and every form of أَخَذْتُ and اتَّخَذْتُ, such as أَخَذتُّمْ (3:81), لَئِنِ اتَّخَذتَّ (26:29) and فَأَخَذتُّهُمْ. Ḥafṣ reads iẓhār in all of them.

Dāl into dhāl and thāʾ: the dāl of ṣād is merged into the dhāl in كٓهيعٓصٓ ذِّكْرُ (19:1–2), the hāʾ there being read without imālah, and the dāl is merged into the thāʾ in يُرِد ثَّوَابَ (3:145). Ḥafṣ reads iẓhār in both.
Nūn of يسٓ and نٓ: when joining, the nūn is merged into the wāw in يسٓ وَالْقُرْآنِ (36:1–2) and نٓ وَالْقَلَمِ (68:1); Ḥafṣ reads iẓhār.
Thāʾ before tāʾ: the Durrah study adds that he reads لَبِثْتُ in all its forms and أُورِثْتُمُوهَا (7:43, 43:72) with iẓhār, like Ḥafṣ.

chapters.title: Nūn sākinah and tanwīn
paragraphs: Before wāw and yāʾ: idghām with ghunnah, as in مَن يَقُولُ (2:8) and مِن وَالٍ (13:11), like Ḥafṣ.

chapters.title: Fatḥ and imālah
paragraphs: Dhawāt al-yāʾ: he reads with major imālah every final alif that goes back to a yāʾ, in nouns and verbs, when a vowelled letter follows or when he stops: أَدْنَىٰ, تَوَلَّىٰ, الْهَوَىٰ. Ḥafṣ reads all such words with fatḥ.

Word patterns: the feminine alif is inclined in the patterns fuʿlā, faʿlā and fiʿlā, as in الدُّنْيَا, مُوسَىٰ, التَّقْوَىٰ, الْمَوْتَىٰ, إِحْدَى and عِيسَىٰ, and in fuʿālā and faʿālā, as in كُسَالَىٰ and الْيَتَامَىٰ.
Verse endings: the dhawāt al-yāʾ at the ends of the āyāt are inclined in eleven sūrahs: Ṭāhā, al-Najm, al-Maʿārij, al-Qiyāmah, al-Nāziʿāt, ʿAbasa, al-Aʿlā, al-Shams, al-Layl, al-Ḍuḥā and al-ʿAlaq.
Other inclined words: among those the source lists are الرِّبَا, الضُّحَىٰ, الْقُوَىٰ, الْعُلَىٰ, كِلَاهُمَا, إِنَاهُ, مُزْجَاةٍ and تُقَاةً (3:28).

رَأَىٰ: both the rāʾ and the hamzah are inclined, as in رَأَىٰ كَوْكَبًا (6:76). Before a sākin, as in رَأَى الْقَمَرَ (6:77) and رَأَى الشَّمْسَ (6:78), the source marks the rāʾ as inclined when joining, and the hamzah is inclined only when stopping on the word.

Dhawāt al-rāʾ: the alif after rāʾ is inclined in بُشْرَىٰ, أُخْرَىٰ, ذِكْرَىٰ, النَّصَارَىٰ and the like. He also inclines التَّوْرَاةَ, which Ḥamzah reads with taqlīl, and الرُّؤْيَا when it carries the definite article, which Ḥamzah reads with fatḥ; رُؤْيَا, رُؤْيَاكَ and رُؤْيَايَ remain with fatḥ.
Alif between two rāʾs: inclined when the second rāʾ carries a kasrah: الْأَبْرَارِ (3:193), الْأَشْرَارِ (38:62), دَارُ الْقَرَارِ (40:39), ذَاتِ قَرَارٍ (23:50). Ḥamzah reads these with taqlīl.
Three-letter past verbs: of the ten verbs that Ḥamzah inclines, Khalaf inclines only three, جَاءَ, شَاءَ and رَانَ; the other seven he reads with fatḥ.
Letters opening the sūrahs: the source marks imālah of the rāʾ in الٓر and الٓمٓر, the ḥāʾ in حمٓ, the ṭāʾ in طسٓمٓ, and طه.

Fatḥ before a final rāʾ with kasrah: there is no imālah in النَّارِ, النَّهَارِ, الدَّارِ, الْجَارِ and جَبَّارِينَ, as for Ḥafṣ. He likewise reads الْقَهَّارِ, الْبَوَارِ (14:28) and ضِعَافًا (4:9) with fatḥ, departing from Ḥamzah.

Words inclined by al-Kisāʾī alone: Khalaf reads them with fatḥ: مَرْضَاتِ, خَطَايَاكُمْ, مَحْيَاهُمْ (45:21), حَقَّ تُقَاتِهِ (3:102), وَقَدْ هَدَانِ (6:80), وَمَنْ عَصَانِي (14:36), أَنسَانِيهِ (18:63), ءَاتَانِيَ الْكِتَابَ (19:30), وَأَوْصَانِي (19:31), and the verse endings سَجَىٰ (93:2), دَحَاهَا (79:30), تَلَاهَا (91:2) and طَحَاهَا (91:6).

Alif before a sākin: when the inclined alif is dropped in joining because a sākin follows, there is no imālah; it returns only on stopping. This covers words with tanwīn such as سُوًى (20:58), مُسَمًّى, أَذًى, طُوًى and سُدًى (75:36), and words before another sākin such as مُوسَى الْكِتَابَ, عِيسَى ابْنِ مَرْيَمَ, الْقَتْلَى الْحُرُّ (2:178) and ذِكْرَى الدَّارِ (38:46).

chapters.title: Waqf
paragraphs: Hāʾ al-sakt dropped in joining: in لَمْ يَتَسَنَّهْ (2:259) and اقْتَدِهْ (6:90) he pronounces the hāʾ only when stopping and drops it when joining, reading لَمْ يَتَسَنَّ وَانظُرْ and اقْتَدِ قُل. Ḥafṣ keeps it in both states.

Hāʾ al-sakt kept: in the other five words, كِتَابِيَهْ, حِسَابِيَهْ, مَالِيَهْ and سُلْطَانِيَهْ in al-Ḥāqqah (69:19–29) and مَا هِيَهْ (101:10), he keeps the hāʾ both when joining and when stopping, like Ḥafṣ. In the last three Ḥamzah drops it when joining.
Stopping on hamzah and on inclined words: the hamzah is kept with taḥqīq, and an alif whose imālah was lost before a sākin is inclined again on stopping, as described in the chapters above.

chapters.title: Yāʾāt al-iḍāfah
paragraphs: Before hamzat al-qaṭʿ: the yāʾ is sākinah and is lengthened four ḥarakāt as madd munfaṣil: وَأُمِّي إِلَٰهَيْنِ (5:116), يَدِي إِلَيْكَ (5:28), مَعِي أَبَدًا (9:83), مَعِي أَوْ رَحِمَنَا (67:28), أَجْرِي إِلَّا. Ḥafṣ reads these particular examples with fatḥ, وَأُمِّيَ, يَدِيَ, مَعِيَ, أَجْرِيَ.
Before hamzat al-waṣl without the lām of definition: sākinah, so it falls away in joining: مِن بَعْدِي اسْمُهُ (61:6), قَوْمِي اتَّخَذُوا (25:30), like Ḥafṣ.

Before the lām of definition: of the fourteen places he reads twelve with fatḥ, such as عَهْدِيَ الظَّالِمِينَ (2:124), which Ḥafṣ reads with sukūn, ءَاتَانِيَ الْكِتَابَ (19:30) and مَسَّنِيَ الضُّرُّ (21:83). The two vocative places he reads with sukūn: يَا عِبَادِي الَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا (29:56) and يَا عِبَادِي الَّذِينَ أَسْرَفُوا (39:53), where Ḥafṣ reads fatḥ. Ḥamzah reads all fourteen with sukūn.

Before any other letter: of the thirty places he reads twenty-eight with sukūn, where Ḥafṣ opens a number of them; one has fatḥ, وَمَحْيَايَ (6:162), and in one the yāʾ is dropped, يَا عِبَادِ لَا خَوْفٌ (43:68).

chapters.title: Yāʾāt al-zawāʾid
paragraphs: General rule: Khalaf drops every extra yāʾ, both when joining and when stopping.
فَمَا ءَاتَانِ اللَّهُ (27:36): he drops the yāʾ here too, whereas Ḥafṣ pronounces it with fatḥ when joining, ءَاتَانِيَ اللَّهُ.
The two yāʾs of Ḥamzah: he also drops the yāʾ in وَتَقَبَّلْ دُعَاءِ (14:40) and in أَتُمِدُّونَنِ (27:36), the two places where Ḥamzah keeps it.

chapters.title: Notable individual words
paragraphs: Ishmām of ṣād before dāl: like Ḥamzah, he gives every sākin ṣād followed by dāl a sound mixed with zāy: وَمَنْ أَصْدَقُ (4:87), يَصْدِفُونَ (6:46), تَصْدِيَةً (8:35), تَصْدِيقَ (10:37, 12:111), فَاصْدَعْ (15:94), قَصْدُ السَّبِيلِ (16:9), يُصْدِرَ (28:23). Ḥafṣ reads a pure ṣād.
بِمُصَيْطِرٍ and الْمُصَيْطِرُونَ: according to the Durrah study he reads بِمُصَيْطِرٍ (88:22) and الْمُصَيْطِرُونَ (52:37) with a pure ṣād, without ishmām.

First of two sākins: when the second sākin begins a verb with hamzat al-waṣl whose third letter has a permanent ḍammah, he gives the first sākin a ḍammah: قُلُ ادْعُوا اللَّهَ أَوُ ادْعُوا الرَّحْمَٰنَ (17:110), قَالَتُ اخْرُجْ (12:31), أَنُ اعْبُدُوا, وَلَقَدُ اسْتُهْزِئَ (6:10), and the tanwīn in مَحْظُورًا ٱنظُرْ (17:20–21). Ḥafṣ reads a kasrah in all of these.
يَحْسِبُ: the sīn of the present tense has kasrah wherever it occurs, تَحْسِبُ, يَحْسِبُونَ, يَحْسِبُهُمْ (2:273); Ḥafṣ reads fatḥ, يَحْسَبُ.
رَءُوفٌ: read short, without the wāw of madd, لَرَؤُفٌ; Ḥafṣ reads لَرَءُوفٌ.
يَا بُنَيِّ: with kasrah of the yāʾ; Ḥafṣ reads يَا بُنَيَّ with fatḥ.
Kasrah of the first letter: الْبِيُوتَ and بِيُوتًا with kasrah of the bāʾ, and نِسْيًا (19:23) with kasrah of the nūn; Ḥafṣ reads الْبُيُوتَ and نَسْيًا.

Other words read differently from Ḥafṣ: لَمَسْتُمُ النِّسَاءَ (4:43, 5:6) without alif, where Ḥafṣ reads لَامَسْتُمُ; تُمَاسُّوهُنَّ (2:236), where Ḥafṣ reads تَمَسُّوهُنَّ; تَسَّاقَطْ (19:25), where Ḥafṣ reads تُسَاقِطْ; تَلَقَّفُ (7:117), where Ḥafṣ reads تَلْقَفُ; ثَمُودًا with tanwīn, as in أَلَا إِنَّ ثَمُودًا (11:68), where Ḥafṣ reads ثَمُودَ; and the singular الرِّيحَ in places where Ḥafṣ reads the plural الرِّيَاحَ.

doubts: The primary source does not treat the istiʿādhah, and gives only waṣl without basmalah between two sūrahs (no sakt); nothing more is stated here.

The primary source states no difference between Isḥāq and Idrīs anywhere in the uṣūl. It says Khalaf has no sakt; the only mention of Idrīs's sakt is a footnote in the Durrah study saying it is read for Idrīs by the Ṭayyibah, not the Durrah. The Sakt chapter is written on that basis.
لِأَهْلِهِ امْكُثُوا: the primary gives the sūrahs as '20, 27, 29'; the phrase occurs in Ṭāhā 20:10 and al-Qaṣaṣ 28:29 (as the Durrah study says), so those references were used.
ءَأَٰمَنتُمْ: the primary gives the sūrahs as '7, 20, 27'; the third place is al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:49 (as the Durrah study says), so that reference was used.

إِنَّكُمْ لَتَأْتُونَ الرِّجَالَ in al-Aʿrāf 7:81: the primary cites only the two places in al-ʿAnkabūt, while the Durrah study says Khalaf reads 7:81 as a statement 'opposing his base'; this looks doubtful, so 7:81 was left out.
The primary mentions طَيْف / طَائِف (7:201) next to يُضَاهُونَ under 'dropped hamzah', but the text is garbled and it is not clear which form is meant for Khalaf; it was left out.

Imālah lists in the primary are inconsistent: عَصَانِي and هَدَانِي appear both in the list of inclined words and in the list of al-Kisāʾī-only words that Khalaf reads with fatḥ. The explicit statement was followed (fatḥ in وَقَدْ هَدَانِ 6:80 and وَمَنْ عَصَانِي 14:36). The differences from Ḥamzah (taqlīl/fatḥ) in the imālah chapter come from the Durrah study.

رَأَى before a sākin, and the imālah of the opening letters, are taken from the imālah markings in the primary's machine-extracted Arabic rather than from an explicit English statement; the primary says only that the hamzah is inclined on stopping, and that the hāʾ of كهيعص has no imālah.

بِمُصَيْطِرٍ / الْمُصَيْطِرُونَ: the primary lists them among the ishmām words (attributing the ishmām to Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī), but the farsh table of the Durrah study says Khalaf reads both with ṣād without ishmām; the latter was followed.

عُيُون, شُيُوخًا, الْغُيُوب, جُيُوبِهِنَّ: the primary lists these with kasrah of the first letter together with بِيُوت and نِسْيًا, but the Durrah study's farsh table gives Khalaf ḍammah in these four (kasrah only in بِيُوت). They were therefore omitted from the kasrah rule.

From the primary's closing list of words 'read differently from Ḥafṣ', يَبْشُرُ, الرُّعُبَ and وُلْدًا were omitted: no place is given, and the Durrah study shows Khalaf reading وَلَدًا with fatḥ everywhere except Sūrat Nūḥ; the other two could not be confirmed. For الرِّيحَ the source gives no list of places.

Iẓhār of the lām of hal/bal, iẓhār of tāʾ al-taʾnīth before thāʾ, and taḥqīq of hamzah on stopping are indicated in the primary only through quoted verses of the Durrah; the plain statements come from the Durrah study. The rule on لَبِثْتُ and أُورِثْتُمُوهَا comes from the Durrah study alone, in a sentence that also (apparently by mistake) lists عُذْتُ under iẓhār; idghām of عُذتُّ was kept, as both sources state elsewhere.
قَوْمِي اتَّخَذُوا (25:30): the Durrah study says in one sentence that Khalaf opens the yāʾ, but its own summary and the primary both give sukūn before hamzat al-waṣl; sukūn was followed.

Surah:ayah references not printed in the primary (for example for the idghām examples, جَبْرَئِيلَ, مِيكَائِيلَ, دَكَّاءَ in 7:143, and the examples for nūn sākinah and lām of hal/bal) were supplied from the Quranic text.
